#3749. How to change layers in WoW Forever? (After the layer size change)

If you want to play with friends in WoW: Forever, you have to go back to one of WoW's most dreaded concepts - layers and shards.

World of Warcraft: Forever skips realms and introduces gameplay rulesets instead, where you can pick your preferred playstyle and get whisked to an Azeroth populated with like-minded individuals. But things can get complicated if, say, you want to play with your friends or guildmates from across the world.

Plus, it’s not like Blizzard will squeeze everyone using your gameplay ruleset into the same world instance. This is where layers come in, and it’s similar to, but also very different from, its original iteration in Classic.

Others new to WoW might be wondering what exactly layers are, and how they might affect their WoW: Forever experience.

So we know MMOs have servers, and each WoW server has a realm that contains a version of Azeroth and the players inside it. Of course, we can’t expect Blizzard to spawn everyone at once, since we’d overcrowd the game world and break the experience.

When a location gets a high-enough population, WoW uses sharding to copy the area into a “shard” and transfers some players there. A shard is a perfectly working copy of a location, complete with NPCs and objects, except you can only see and interact with players of the same shard.

The idea is to manage overpopulation by keeping player counts at a certain number. This keeps lag manageable and ensures there are enough mobs and quest items for everyone in any given zone.

Since shards are zone-wide, you can see players “disappear” into a new zone because they’re crossing over to a new shard (called phasing). If you’re approaching a zone where all shards are at capacity, you’d hit a soft “loading” queue before you enter. Worst case, you get disconnected from the server, which can ruin your momentum.

WoW Retail still uses sharding. It sometimes implements cross-realm zones (CRZs), so low-population realms can share low-population zones.

We got to layering at the launch of WoW Classic in 2019, where it was presented as a bigger solution to server population. Sharding at the time just didn’t feel like a practical choice, as they’d have to create hundreds of shards per zone.

“We had some serious concerns about what would happen when realms started to mature, and populations shifted,” Blizzard noted about sharding in the release of Battle for Wintergrasp in Wrath Classic. “Would we have hundreds of realms with low populations a few months in?”

So they came up with layers, which is sharding but applied to the whole game world. Upon meeting specific population conditions, Blizzard can create a copy of Azeroth and transfer players there.

But it’s not a perfect solution. Too much layering could result in dead cities, and too little overcrowds areas. It can hurt the economy as well, as you can layer-hop to get more resources from another layer once your layer’s route runs out.

Classic moved away from layering just a few months in November 2019 and converged everyone into a single layer.

Read what’s behind the latest news in gaming (with a bit of snark) by subscribing to the Destructoid Checkpoint newsletter!

Players reintroduced the layering and sharding discourse back into Forever overpopulation concerns during launch. We don’t have the full picture of how Blizzard is managing Forever servers as of writing, but players seem to have noticed enough to make informed assumptions:

Instead of realms, we choose a ruleset that represents our preferred playstyle and play with others who choose the same. In theory, it’s a “realmless” system, and our ruleset of choice is functionally a mega server that our fellow ruleset comrades share.

Forever seems to have retained the Retail sharding system. But this time, there’s a chance you can auto-switch layers during the transition. This seems to have carried over from beta. Redditor u/Kellian noted that per-zone “loading” means hostiles and friendlies phase in and out, and can even stop PvP.

Building upon the ruleset is what Blizzard called the familiar faces system. As explained in their BlizzCon 2026 deep-dive, this will have players more consistently encounter the same strangers throughout their leveling journey. The goal is for these familiar faces to give Forever a stronger sense of community spirit, and may even encourage teaming up while you level. This also extends to guilds, so they can potentially pull you into their layers.

At random intervals during your sessions (sometimes none at all), you might encounter a prompt that warns you of a World Refresh. Either you do the refresh now or wait a couple of minutes. This isn’t any cause for alarm, as it just means the game will transfer you to a new instance or layer.

These refreshes often happen to balance the current population. You remain in the same spot, but your immediate surroundings might be different, like there might be more players, more mobs, or both.

Switching between layers in Forever can be done in a variety of ways, but there’s no manual options button to do so. Instead, you can do some things to “force” your way into a layer switch. Popular methods you can try include:

At launch, game dev Aggrend said they would look into how players lamented how sparsely populated the game world felt. A few days later, some players noticed so many characters for so few mobs.

This was especially challenging in PvP, where one faction can dominate a layer and make it difficult for the opposing one to level up or gather resources.

Redditor u/sknilegap doesn’t even call it layering at all, but actually just sharding. And their problem has less to do with the technology itself, but more with its impact on the experience at large.

“I am fine with the necessity of the system. Just keep it immersive,” they said in their post. “Make me sticky to those crossing over around the same time window as me. So […] we all see each other on the other side of the next zone, grouped or not.”

You can play World of Warcraft: Forever on PC and macOS.

I really wasn't expecting Microsoft Paint to turn up in the cybersecurity headlines, but here we are. MS disclosed and patched a security vulnerability within the software on October 13, but it's worth checking your own Paint version to see if you've received the update.

Some users don't have automatic Microsoft Store updates enabled, especially those on work machines. As Paint is updated via the store, you may need to manually update to version 11.2609.401.0 to keep your machine secure.

To confuse things further, International Cyber Digest reports that the MS store was providing older versions to some users until recently, and Windows Latest didn't seem to receive the new version even with auto updates enabled. Or, there's been some mixup with release numbers. It's genuinely difficult to tell at this point, with differing information coming from multiple sources.

The vulnerability was initially given an 8.1 severity rating on the CVSS scale, but Microsoft downgraded it to a 7.0 score on November 9 according to Threat Defence. MS also changed its description of the bug to that of a local exploit (requiring a user to open a crafted file) rather than a network attack vector, .

Regardless, to check whether your Paint version is hopefully up-to-date (what a world we live in), open the app, go to the Settings menu, and check the version number beneath the "About Paint" section. If it's lower than version 11.2609.401.0, open the Microsoft Store and manually update the app. Or, if your Windows 11 settings don't allow user updates, contact your sysadmin.

You can also check your Paint version within Windows Powershell by running:

Honestly, this is the biggest omnishambles of conflicting cybersecurity info I've seen in a while. Some outlets initially reported the bug as a no-click security flaw, while others have suggested that the vulnerability could potentially be exploited via a specially crafted image. Microsoft shifting the security goalposts as it goes really hasn't helped, nor has its apparently messy roll out of the patched version.

#3747. "Something's really possible" - Mass Effect cast rally around efforts to save the franchise on the first N7 Day after BioWare's closure

I'm Commander Shepard and this is my favorite video on the internet.

This N7 Day was the first without developer BioWare around, but fans of the Mass Effect series didn't let 7th November go by quietly. The community managed to get several notable Mass Effect actors to lend their voice to the increasingly loud 'SaveMassEffect' movement.

In the weeks since BioWare's shock closure and Mass Effect Universe's cancellation, the community-organised We Are Mass Effect group have put up billboards in Times Square, a mobile billboard outside BioWare Edmonton's former office and much more while directing attention to an online petition.

Today is a very special day for Mass Effect fans. We've worked incredibly hard to bring together most of the original Mass Effect trilogy's voice cast to share a very important message with you. We need to #SaveMassEffect. https://t.co/FOp0qp4wBI

And for the series' annual celebration, the group managed to get a sizable portion of the Mass Effect cast to join in. Commander Shepard actors Jennifer Hale and Mark Meer, original trilogy composer Sam Hulick, Garrus' Brandon Keener, Jack's Courtnay Taylor, Tali'Zorah's Ash Sroka, Thane's Keythe Farley and many more all showed up in a two-minute video to help potentially salvage the series - sometimes in character.

"When we heard about the formal closing of Boware, I felt weirdly hopeful," Hale said in a separate interview with IGN. "I can't explain it. I just got so weirdly hopeful. My first thought, of course, was for the devs and all the people. And then I just closed my eyes and crossed my fingers and I said, 'I feel something's possible. You know, something's really possible.'"

The other half of Commander Shepard, Mark Meer, noted that "this didn't all just happen in the last 10 days." Near yearly layoffs at EA had slowly trimmed multiple BioWare teams down, sometimes even affecting studio veterans who had been at the company for decades.

"A lot of senior writers within the last year or two were let go. People who had been there from the very beginning. Again, people who had built that company from the ground up, who built the bones of it, who made those games that had captured people so much right back from the 1990s," Meer said.

Henry Cavill is never afraid to get his geek on, and I love that for him. More importantly, he’s not afraid to do so while raising awareness for an important cause. All this month, the Movember Foundation is raising money for and shining a light on important topics in men’s health, from cancer awareness to mental health support. So naturally, this means Cavill is back with a mustache for Movember (and totally pulls it off).

The Superman actor is a long time supporter of the foundation, having previously grown a mustache in support. This time, the actor is embracing his nerdy side as his latest team up pairs him with Google’s Antigravity (an AI tool on Googlebook) to create a 16-bit game called “Mustache Protocol.” In it, a suspiciously Cavill-looking mustachioed hero is making his mission to stop rogue CGI artists from erasing all the mustaches in the world. The actor post Part 2 (of a three part series) on his Instagram:

A post shared by Henry Cavill (@henrycavill)

As you can see, the hero has lots of muscles and a handlebar mustache very similar to the Witcher actor’s own fancy ‘stache. While the attention should be primarily on raising awareness for Movemeber, it’s hard to miss the cheeky humor presented in the video, specifically the arm re-load. Now, you maybe thinking, "huh, that looks a little familiar." Well, you’d be right. This is a fun nod to Cavill’s role in Mission Impossible - Fallout, which fans helpfully dropped in the comments in the form of gifs. You know, in case you needed reminding.

Paramount has previously used the mustache in that movie when the studio made a donation to the Movember Foundation. However, that’s not what Cavill is winking at in the video. He dropped an “IYKYK” when giving his hero a “little pocket,” which if you know, is another Mission Impossible reference. If you don’t, this is slightly poking fun at continuity errors in the movie, which yes, included disappearing pockets, but fans are here for the 'stache:

The actor is clearly having fun taking a break from several projects, including a Highlander reboot movie, and doing so for a worthy cause. Though I wasn’t surprised to see the style of the game had a delightful vintage feel to it. The stylistic choices really show off Cavill’s personality, and that’s why fans are loving the videos. Only he could make brisket feel like a reasonable health choice for a power up. Part of the joy in watching the actor create something so wholesome is seeing him show off his wonderfully geeky side, which fans get to see often. Surely the “game of the year awards” is Cavill’s for the taking, right?

Whether it’s his love of the Witcher video games or working with Amazon on the Warhammer 40,000 series, he’s never strayed from being just like the rest of us. He’s also reportedly attached to the Voltron live action adaptation of the animated series from the ‘80s. Though I have no information on whether or not he'll have a fancy 'stache.

I mustache you to remember that while you're supporting all of these projects, that you also check out the foundation's website and note the importance of the 'stache this Movember.

I'll be the first to admit I've said some incredibly questionable-sounding things while playing videogames. Or talking about them in public. But I would like to think that the one place where I would be extra careful about the words coming out of my mouth are in an airport, or on an airplane. Really, anywhere with an insane amount of security and an ever-pervasive fear of anything explosives-related.

Unfortunately, for passengers on board a Frontier Airlines flight earlier this week, however, one such gamer was not so cautious. As reported by CBS News, one plane at California's Ontario International Airport had to be evacuated over a bomb scare, only for it to be some guy playing Call of Duty with his pal.

According to reports, one passenger overheard words such as "bomb" and "explosion" and, rightly so, went and told staff about it. The situation led to both the plane and the east wing of Terminal 2 being evacuated, and a check of the aircraft which revealed that no explosives or bombs were on board.

After detaining and speaking to the culprit, it was revealed that he was, in fact, on FaceTime with his buddy while playing Call of Duty together. He was released without any charges, and the flight was reboarded and departed later that night.

I do feel a little bad for laughing about it—as a nervous flyer, I know for a fact that if I had been that passenger overhearing the conversation I may very well have gone into full-blown panic mode. I don't even like when someone doesn't put their phone on airplane mode as we're taking off!

But I'm also the type of person to watch my friend's Discord streams while I'm out and about, and I honestly dread to think about the kind of things passerbys have heard me say while spectating games. #3743. GTA 6 pre-orders are tracking "well above expectations" and the game will "set a new baseline" for Take-Two, says CEO Strauss Zelnick

Today, as part of Take-Two Interactive Software's Q2 2027 earnings call, Strauss Zelnick noted that pre-orders for Grand Theft Auto 6 are tracking "far above expectations", and is certain that soon "numbers will speak for themselves" when it comes to the game.

Zelnick also promised GTA Online and GTA 5 will continue to receive updates in order to support the "nearly 235 million" units sold to date across "an unprecedented three console generations". The GTA series as a whole has, to date, sold over 480 million units. Karl Statoff, president at Take-Two, adds the launch of GTA 6 will be a "defining moment for the company and global entertainment industry". Zelnick adds, later in a question and answer session, that he expects GTA 6 to "set a new baseline" for Take-Two. "The future's really bright across the board," he notes.

For the next quarter, Take-Two expects to deliver $3.35 billion to $3.5 billion - with "recurrent consumer spending" to raise by 12 percent, driven by "the groundbreaking release" of Grand Theft Auto 6, and expects to see "significant growth for the Grand Theft Auto series", driven by sales of - specifically - Grand Theft Auto 6's Ultimate Edition, which includes add-on content, and that most people are pre-ordering at its $100 price point. That bonus $20 between the $80 base edition and the Ultimate Edition is counted as "recurrent consumer spending", as is part of that massive bump the company has seen.

It also seems that we will see more GTA games - or content, at least - sooner than expected. "We do think that the nature and velocity of the content we'll see from our iconic franchises, including GTA, will look dramatically different over the next decade." It's a vague comment, but assumedly the work done on the engine and backend of GTA 6 means we'll see more content arriving in shorter order than we're used to for the series. This is per an article published by IGN in line with the earning's call going live.

Elsewhere in the earnings call, Take-Two referred to its current setup with its mobile, sports, 'core new IP' and 'core existing IP' as "the strongest development pipeline in the company's history". In terms of new IP, Zelnick directed investors to consider the launches of incoming projects like Ken Levine's mysterious Judas and Project Ethos (which we don't know too much about yet, other than it's billed as a "roguelike hero shooter"). For core IP, 8 sequels and 7 remakes, remasters, and platform extensions.

Buoyed by these plans, Zelnick outlines that he believes that fiscal year 2027 "will be a historic year for Take-Two" as the company is buoyed by "recent and upcoming releases". No prizes for what that's referring to. If you're curious about what sort of numbers we may be looking at here, all you need to do is cast your mind back to 2014, where you will remember GTA 5 made $1bn in just three days.

#3742. Zelda: Ocarina Of Time Remake Has A Massive Second-Act Change That Took My Breath Away

Nintendo Switch 2The Legend of ZeldaThe Legend of Zelda: Ocarina Of Time

Last night in my playthrough of Ocarina of Time, I finished up the Fire Temple and headed (as one does) to Zora Domain, expecting it to be (as the rest of the game has been so far) very much like the original in structure, just visually more elaborate. And it was, mostly. But as I passed through the realm, I also encountered one of my favorite new additions to the remake so far, one that simultaneously clears up one of Ocarina of Time‘s long-enduring inconsistencies, while also adding pretty significant elements of both horror and hope to the original story.

In the original Ocarina of Time, Zora Domain in the adult timeline is completely frozen over. When Link enters, there are no Zora to be foundâjust an iced-over pond and a frozen waterfall. At the top, you can find King Zora, encased in red ice. Through your adventures in Ice Cavern and later Water Temple, you learn that Ganondorf is (of course) responsible, and that all the Zora have been completely frozen. Sheik was able to save Ruto, who goes on to become the Sage of Water, and you’re later able to thaw out King Zora using Blue Fire.

But the fate of the rest of the Zora is sort of…ambiguous. Presumably due to technical limitations in the original, Zora Domain in adult timeline remains frozen over even post-Water Temple, and the Zora people are nowhere to be found. It’s just King Zora, sitting on his icy throne, for the rest of the game, and Ruto now effectively dead to the world in the Sacred Realm as a sage. You do see some Zora in the credits sequence at the end of the game, implying that some survived, but just what happened to Hyrule’s aquatic folk more broadly remains pretty murky.

The remake clears that up, but the way it does this made me say “holy shit”Â out loud several times.

When you enter Zora Domain as adult Link, you’re treated to a souped-up version of the same sight: frozen pond, frozen waterfall, frozen everything. New to the remake is a haunting new piece of music that does a great job of conveying the frozen emptiness you’re faced with. I hate that you can occasionally hear snippets of the main Zora theme instruments creeping in between the weird, spooky noises! Agh!

But even worse (read: better) than this is what you see when you go out onto the pond. And look down. Into the ice.

Uh, yeah. That’s what that is. That’s where they are. They are actively frozen beneath their own pond. You can just. See them. Down there. Trapped. Dead? Effectively tortured by cold?! Holy shit.

I haven’t finished the Water Temple yet. I considered waiting until I had finished it to write this blog, but I decided to write it now because I wanted to talk about the other emotion, aside from horror, that seeing this inspired. If the Zora are in there now, that opens the door for them to be freed when I finish Water Temple. There are no technical limitations prohibiting Nintendo from thawing out Zora Domain when the time comes and giving these people their lives back. Can Ruto and I really, truly, conclusively save the Zora this time around?

Right now, I am loving the anticipation! I can’t wait to finish the Water Temple tonight, and while I’m a little afraid of being disappointed by the outcome in case Nintendo decided to leave the Zora in this horrible frozen state until the credits, the overall excellence and attention to detail of the Ocarina of Time remake so far has given me ample reason for hope.

Some spoilers for A Dog’s Perfect Christmas can be found in this piece

Christmas movies have officially hit the 2026 TV Schedule and taken over my life. Between Hallmark’s Countdown to Christmas, Netflix, and even Hulu, the new Christmas movie options are endless. It can be hard to decide what to watch, and when I saw the trailer for Netflix’s A Dog’s Perfect Christmas, I knew it had to be moved to the top of my list, even if I was sure it was going to make me cry.

The book-to-screen adaptation centered on the Goss family during a difficult holiday season when Juliana (Kathleen Rose Perkins) fell ill, leaving her workaholic husband (Milo Ventimiglia) and depressed father-in-law (Dennis Quaid) in charge of their teenage daughter (Brooke Lena Johnson), rambunctious twins, and beloved basset hound. The film was largely narrated by Winstead the beloved basset hound, and also included an adorable corgi puppy that Ello, the teenage daughter, rescued from the streets.

A Dog’s Perfect Christmas had something for everyone: adorable dogs, family drama, and even romance. I knew it was going to be an emotional watch from the start, but I couldn’t have imagined what led me to reach for the tissues over and over again.

I don’t think I’m the only one who immediately worries for a dog’s safety when they’re in a movie. Hollywood has a long history of killing beloved family dogs, so much so that there are entire websites dedicated to finding out if a movie contains a pet death. I’m someone who doesn’t like spoilers, though, so I’ve always refrained from checking it out, which is why I spent a large chunk of A Dog’s Perfect Christmas terrified for Winstead.

The odds were stacked against Winstead from the start. He was old, his human was already depressed about losing his wife, and the teenage daughter had brought a new puppy into the home. Plus, Winstead made it clear that his goal was to make his human (Quaid) find happiness again. The closer he got to that goal, the more I started to worry for his fate.

Thankfully, Winstead was spared from a tragic Hollywood ending, and so was Ruby, the adorable corgi puppy who officially becomes a member of the family by the end.

Netflix spared me from sobbing over a dead dog, but I still shed several tears while watching A Dog’s Perfect Christmas. Watching the family have to deal with Juliana’s illness was heartbreaking, especially knowing that they had already gone through a huge loss a couple of years prior. I couldn’t help but get teary-eyed when Hunter and Sander had to sit Ello down and explain how sick her mom really was.

While there were plenty of sad tears shed over the course of the film, there were also several times I found myself crying because I was laughing so hard. That was all thanks to Winstead. Even though the dog didn’t die, I still ended up shedding a few years about him anyway.

As the trailer suggested, Winstead was the pseudo-narrator of the film, introducing audiences to the Goss family and keeping us up to date. Of course, he did all this from his dog perspective, which led to some hilarious and touching moments. For example, he referred to Juliana as Juliana-Mom since that’s what he heard everyone calling her, and Christmas became “Merry Christmastime.”

The moments that made me cry from laughter, though, were anytime Winstead intervened to try and bring the family together, but ended up making a mess instead. He yanked a tablecloth off to get Sander and Ello to help each other clean up, and he regularly got the twins hyper in the hopes of making Sander smile.

Any dog owner will recognize the look of a dog who thinks they’re helping but is actually making things worse, and that’s exactly what Winstead did time and time again. I also couldn’t help but get teary-eyed from laughter every time Winstead judged Ruby for making a puppy mistake.

Before you return to the classics and watch one of the best Christmas movies of all time, check out A Dog’s Perfect Christmas, streaming now for everyone with a Netflix subscription. And don’t forget to check out all the upcoming Christmas movies still coming this holiday season.

#3739. As investors ask about GTA 6 and AI, Take-Two CEO once again puts faith in dev creativity, states making hit games "remains the purview of human beings"

"Making a big hit was hard then, and it's hard now, and it's going to be hard in the future."

Today, as part of Take-Two Interactive Software's Q2 2027 earnings call, Strauss Zelnick fielded questions from investors after presenting the financial results of the company. One caller was concerned about AI - specifically about the proliferation of AI-powered compilations and decompilations that have been raising piracy concerns for publishers over the past few weeks.

Zelnick notes that "[the video games] business has been largely immune to piracy" thanks to factors like file size, how console ecosystems work, and aspects related to the online nature of the games industry. That said, Strauss continues, there is a threat posed to the industry because of AI. However, he assures listening investors that Take-Two is appropriately scaling its measures against bad faith actors using artificial intelligence.

"We are utterly focused on enhancing our technical defences and enhancing our legal activities appropriately. And - at the same time, without in any way being cavalier - every entertainment business that exists is subject to some element of piracy, [and] this is likely to invade our business to a greater or lesser extent. I think it will be manageable and we are focused on it."

Zelnick pivots back to AI again later in the call, where one investor once again asks about AI, seemingly keen to learn whether the CEO feels it can provide GTA 6 developer Rockstar with any kind of "competitive advantage" in the games industry. Given Zelnick's previous comments on the subject, his answer was not a complete surprise.

"It's always been true [that technology benefits us]," explains Zelnick. "We've always created our entertainment inside computers with technology. All advances have benefited us, and I don't expect that that will change - in fact, I hope it'll accelerate. I think at the same time, what we're known for [at Take-Two] is the desire to make the best entertainment on Earth. And, more often than not, we have succeeded - and the creativity that drives that success is human creativity harnessing technology. And I think that's what you'll see in the future, too.

"Undoubtedly some of the most recent technological advances that you've seen have made it easier to create assets. Where all that is consistent with the story of our business. When I started in interactive entertainment (longer ago than I would like to say), it was really difficult to create an asset in a computer. Today, it's a whole lot easier - but you know what's not easier? Making a big hit. Making a big hit was hard then, and it's hard now, and it's going to be hard in the future. And hit creation remains the purview of human beings."

This isn't the first instance of AI skepticism we've seen from Strauss Zelnick. Back in March, he outright rejected the idea that AI can tackle games on the scale of GTA 6. Elsewhere in the call, the Take-Two CEO reiterated how well GTA 6 is tracking as he reasserted pre-order numbers are well above expectations, and promised that the success of the game will "set a new baseline" for Take-Two's gaming business.

#3736. Switch 2 and Switch consoles updated to version 23.5.0 as Nintendo quietly re-introduces eShop gifting

Nintendo has just pushed out a new update to all Switch and Switch 2 consoles, bringing the firmware on both up to version 23.5.0. The headline change with the new update is support and compatibility for an upcoming update that will allow members of a Nintendo Account family group to gift games to one another.

The feature itself is expected to go live on 17th November, 2026. "Just in time for the holidays, a new feature will let family group members gift digital games to other members of their group," says a post on a dedicated blog on the Nintendo site. "You will be able to gift digital products that you purchase through Nintendo eShop on your device to family group members. This includes eligible games as well as DLC and upgrade packs. As a reminder, anyone with a Nintendo Account can easily set up a family group and add members (up to 8 total)."

The publisher notes, however, that "some products may not be eligible for digital gifting" and that "supervised accounts are not able to send digital gifts". Additionally, "the number of digital gift purchases allowed in a given period is limited".

"This feature is a great way to celebrate a special occasion with your kids. Happy gifting!" concludes Nintendo. Just in time for the holidays, how thoughtful. It's worth noting that a previous iteration of this support was included back on the Nintendo Wii, but that was much more robust than this - back then, the publisher allowed users to send WiiWare or Virtual Console games to anyone on their Wii Friend list via the Wii Shop Channel, rather than just those limited to their immediate group. This functionality was lost in 2019, alongside the closure of the Wii Shop Channel.

The Legacy System in WoW: Forever turns your account into quite literally a record of your achievements.

Milestones you ordinarily just gloss by become moments that can improve your next playthrough, so the Legacy System is Blizzard’s way of motivating you to get up and get to leveling.

But the Legacy System goes beyond just achieving things. When you finish an objective within the Legacy System, you also earn Legacy Points. And this is spent on buffs all your characters can enjoy. So how exactly should you approach this?

If you can’t see the Legacy System just yet, don’t worry, as it’s locked behind earning your first Legacy Point. This means you’ll unlock it when you reach one of these conditions:

After that, you can access the Legacy System by pressing the “Y” key or the shield icon on the menu.

Just like Achievements in the OG WoW experience, Legacy Challenges in Forever are surprisingly straightforward to accomplish. Here’s a quick rundown on how many possible points you can earn across each category:

Again, Legacy Points are account-wide, so pressure is on to earn these points as soon as possible.

Kim Kardashian is a bona fide billionaire, and that’s in great part due to the performance of her shapewear and clothing brand, SKIMS. The company has seen immense growth and success in recent years, though it now finds itself in a bit of hot water with customers. Just recently, SKIMS dropped its latest advent calendar, and buyers aren’t happy with the items included. The company has since vowed to provide refunds to those who purchased the item but, ahead of that, many took to the Internet to roast this new product from “Kimberly.”

SKIMS has dropped more than a few items over the years that have prompted consumers to splurge, from its signature nipple bras to the more recent “micro fits.” Advent calendars have also been commonly offered by the brand though, and this latest one costs $148. With that price point, buyers were upset to discover that the calendar only included common items like SKIMS-branded bobby pins, hair clips and a small bear keychain. One X user reposted a product review from TikTok, and many users took to the comment section to weigh in:

Comments like these haven’t been limited to X, as some people have also posted about the product on Instagram since its release in early November. One user shared a photo of the calendar and the products and expressed disappointment via their caption:

A post shared by Marina Kelawon (@anthophilic.mermaid)

As mentioned before, though, SKIMS has responded to the situation, as the company shared a statement with Today, saying that it was “aware of the feedback.” The spokesperson confirmed the brand’s intention to provide refunds to dissatisfied customers and also said the following:

We have personally contacted every customer who purchased the calendar and offered them a choice of a full refund or a SKIMS credit to put towards other products. We want every customer to be truly happy with what they receive from SKIMS. Their feedback matters to us and will directly shape how we approach future releases.

This isn’t the first time that SKIMS has been on the receiving end of negatively charged publicity. In 2022, the company received blowback due to a controversy revolving around Kim Kardashian being edited in an ad. 2024 also saw fans outraged due to Kardashian and co. releasing boxers, which many compared to postpartum hospital diapers. A number of people also doubted whether Kardashian was actually modeling the XS size in advertisement materials.

It can’t be said with certainty just how many advent calendars SKIMS has sold this year but, regardless, the company now finds itself in a position to provide some reimbursement. Something that remains unclear at this point, though, is whether Kim Kardashian and her collaborators will choose to make changes to the existing calendar or take this feedback and apply it to the one for next year.

#3732. Switch 2 US sales soar again thanks to The Legend of Zelda effect, as it enjoys its best week of the year so far

Could a remade Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time be exciting enough to revitalise Switch 2 hardware sales? That was the big question. And early sales figures suggest the answer is yes, it can.

The Switch 2, which had been declining in hardware sales over the last few months, just had its highest (dollar) sales week of 2026 in the US so far following the game's release, according to Circana analyst Mat Piscatella on Bluesky.

The accompanying Legend of Zelda: 40th Anniversary Edition console in particular is responsible for a notable jump in Switch 2 hardware dollar sales. The themed, special edition console has been popular, with various retailers immediately running out of stock and a rise in scalping.

It's worth noting that The Legend of Zelda: 40th Anniversary Edition console, priced $520 / £430, does not include a copy of the game. Also, because the console was released 29th October, and the Ocarina of Time remake on 5th November, their sales results will come in separate monthly reports.

The Ocarina of Time launch also caused US hardware spending to jump by 81 percent during the week ending 31st October compared to the same period last year.

Christian Donlan awarded The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time a glitzy five stars in Eurogamer's review, writing: "This is Ocarina as it's always been, as timeless and intricate, but it also has a vibrancy and clarity that makes it feel like it was just created last Wednesday."

If you're currently enjoying the remake, Eurogamer's Ocarina of Time walkthrough is a helpful companion with general tips, items and collectibles guide, quest walkthroughs and more.

I'm modding GTA 5 every day in a quest to either transform it into a PC version of GTA 6 or break it entirely. Come back tomorrow to find out what new horrible thing I've done to Rockstar's baby, or check out what I got up to earlier.

Bring Up The Bodies, often regarded as Hilary Mantel's masterpiece (more of a Place Of Greater Safety man myself), opens thus: "His children are falling from the sky. He watches from horse-back, acres of England stretching behind him; they drop, gilt-winged, each with a blood-filled gaze".

This is a description of Thomas Cromwell's falcons in 1535. It is also a description of the life of Franklin Clinton in 2026. Los Santos is awash in bodies because I have installed PeopleFalling – BloodSky, a mod which sends an endless wave of people plummeting to Earth like a horrible hard rain. "A modification called 'People Falling' or as I call it, 'Blood Sky'", writes the author, confusingly, as they presumably chose both names.

"When you press the 'X' key, characters drop from the sky. You can change the activation button in the .ini file". This is a lie. It's actually the B key. My relationship with PeopleFalling AKA BloodSky got off to a rocky start.

It does work though. Sort of. Tap B (not X) and the rainy season begins—people fall silently to the ground in a kind of reverse-Rapture situation, absolutely all of them physics-free and adopting the same stomach-sleeper position when they finally make contact with sidewalk, with highway, with rooftop.

Then it ends, and no matter how much you tap B—notifications reading "Falling people Active" and "Falling People Deactive" flashing in the lower right of your screen—they never come back. It's like you have witnessed a beautiful, once-in-a-lifetime miracle, like a full solar eclipse or Halley's comet.

Also, when the process is ongoing it really alarms my bodyguard, who responds like a dog hearing a bang in the house at night.

#3729. A Big Talk About Big Walk’s AI Fallout

Big Walk, the game that was likely at or near the top of a lot of people’s game of the year lists, was made in very small part with the use of AI. This was not previously disclosed publicly or on Steam because, according to House House’s statement on the matter, “the platform does not request disclosure of code or chatbot usage.” And we’re only finding out about this now, long after the game has released to universal acclaim, because Big Walk was apparently at the heart of a fractious discussion about AI usage in development and the game’s eligibility for awards among the jury members for the 2027 Independent Games Festival.

Over the past month, IGF judges and jurists have had intense, difficulty, generous, and deeply engaged conversations about AI and the games industry.

This statement is the result of those conversations.

— austin_walker (@austinwalker.bsky.social) 2026-11-09T22:42:15.552Z

Some jurors felt that a hard, no-exceptions line needed to be drawn in the sand, and made a public, signed statement to that effect. Others felt that considering how House House used the tech was worth consideration in determining Big Walk‘s eligibility. House House claims that “well under 0.1% of Big Walkâs code had anything to do with this usage and generative AI was not used in any other context when making the game,” and it seems like some jurors felt that such limited use shouldn’t disqualify a game that was very likely in the running for the Seumas McNally Grand Prize, the IGF’s top award.

The discussions about this event at Kotaku mirror those playing out amongst gamers and developers on social media. But at the heart of it all, this sucks man.

Ash Parrish: Where do you all come down on this? Rebekah Valentine: As the person on this team who went to bat, hard, for this game, who loved it completely, who bullied you all so much to play it and wrote about it incessantly, I will start by saying: God damn it.

Ash: I have not played the game because I havenât taken the time to round up friends to play it with. It was important that I make an effort to try because this game seems so special to everyone Iâve seen talk about it. This whole thing, not just how AI was used but how we found out about it, definitely removes that urgency. Rebekah: I am not naive enough to believe that every game I play has zero AI touching it in any way. In fact, I assume many of them do. But I, and I think many others, made an assumption that based on the past stances of this dev team and their general attention to a lot of hand-crafted detail, AI would not even be a factor.Â

Carolyn Petit: I’m actually playing it right now with friends and it was certainly strange to emerge from our play session last night (for those whoâve played it, we just got the ski lift working!) and into the online discourse. My feeling is that the goal should be an expectation of zero AI usage on any level. It’s stolen labor no matter how you cut it. Does that mean I think House House should be crucified in the court of public opinion? Maybe not, but I do think we need to be clear about establishing and holding to that expectation moving forward, and I donât think it should receive honors at IGF. John Walker: I think itâs really important to recognize that of all the games weâve loved this year, almost all of them will have used LLMs as part of the coding process. I hate that, and I wish they had not, and I appeal to developers to stop doing it. But of all of the games to do this, I suspect Big Walk did it about the very least. So I feel like this is a public flogging that will achieve demoralizing or demolishing a great studio and little else. Ash: Then why not tell us up front and give consumers the choice? I think a lot of people would have been OK with the exact disclosure we were given today. That folks did not have that option to choose feels way worse than the fact AI was used at all. John: I believe the reason why (and again, this isnât my justifying it, but trying to sum up why it happens) is becauseâ¦itâs what everyone does. You run the code through the tool to check for errors. Or you ask the tool to suggest a way to code to fix the issue. And because thatâs the expected action of someone using the coding tools, itâs incredibly easy to forget this is the same world-destroying mechanism that powers the plagiarism art and military drones. Carolyn: Right, but the fact that it’s what everyone does doesn’t mean we should be okay with it. If anything, it’s precisely why we need to be so clear about saying no.

Ash: And weâve got people posting on social media that theyâve seemingly solved the exact problem House House ran into, without using AI.

John: I donât know how much more clearly I can say that I donât think we should be OK with it. Iâm trying to answer the question, âWhy was it used at all?â Carolyn: But you seem to be taking an issue with people taking an issue with it. John: No, Iâm taking an issue with people trying to win an internet battle of virtue by trying to out-hate everyone else, and suggesting that thereâs a better way to convince the vast majority of developers to not do this.

Carolyn: I don’t think we do that without deploying shame to some degree.

John: I find publicly shaming one of the least offending offenders in order to teach the world a lesson a really horrid way to go about discourse. Ash: But wouldnât you agree that having such a public discussion about how this whole thing has gone down is at least an attempt to signal, âHey devs, you donât want this to happen, so donât do thisâ? Like this discussion is the way we try to signal this is not a thing we want and that devs should try to find another way around their problems. And maybe itâs an imperfect way, but itâs something.

Carolyn: Yes. I also think the statement from some jury members was great. And I don’t think we can ignore that this one hurts more than some disposable top-to-bottom AI slop on Steam because of how well-received Big Walk is and because of the dev teamâs commendable stance on things like BDS.

Rebekah: Itâs a really complicated thing to think and talk about and I have a lot of conflicting thoughts here.

On one hand, I share Carolynâs opinion that I want zero AI usage on any level. And I want the industry to take steps toward that. I think the IGF judgesâ statement is a great move to that end, and I support it. More groups, more award shows, should make such statements and stick to such convictions.

I also think I see a bit of what John is saying here and why heâs saying it. I think that House House has generally demonstrated itself to be a group of thoughtful developers (see: the BDS boycott), and their statement now reflects this. This, as Carolyn says, makes what feels like a betrayal more hurtful. But I also do believe them based on past actions when they say they feel not having a policy about this is a failure and that they are going to address that. A lot of the public response Iâve seen to this has been to deem the whole game as slop, to condemn them utterly, and treating this as an irredeemable offense. It sounds like some of the behind-the-scenes discussion on IGF was like that too. And I donât really agree with that. Iâd rather this open a discussion publicly about why they felt this was necessary and help both House House and other devs in their position come around to better ways of doing things. What Iâm afraid will happen instead (and what some seem to be doing already) is that theyâll just get deemed a slop studio and thatâs that. Meanwhile, hundreds of other, bigger studios with far worse morals will skate on by without ever disclosing anything.

Again, to be clear, I donât think we solve that problem by not talking about it and by not shaming it. I reiterate that I am really upset and betrayed by this, a problem that was so easy to avoid! I just wish there were a better way to have industry-wide conversations generally. Bluesky, Twitter, and social media in general donât seem to be it. John: I too want zero AI use! Rebekah: I also want to recognize that Iâm feeling both betrayed by them and maybe a little defensive of them because I loved the game so much. And also that my own view of discussions on social media is incomplete and not reflective of the broader consensus. Iâm not a dev. This stuff is hard, man. Itâs easy to say Iâm anti-AI. The more I try to put it into practice though, the harder it is to do, because this crap keeps popping up everywhere, unexpectedly, unasked for, unwanted.

Ash: And thatâs only the stuff we know about. And I think my genuine disaffection comes from the lack of disclosure.

John: I wonder if any of us manages not to have AI be in at least 0.1 percent of our lives. Every time I search something in the Chrome taskbar and forget itâll be a Gemini screed of gibberish, but with a useful link. Or when I click on the âchat nowâ button on the medical site I use, and have to fight past the AI to get to a person. Ash: I mean thatâs a structural issue, isnât it? Some of us would, if the structures undergirding our lives would allow us, choose to be totally AI-free. We should have at least nominally more power over that in our leisure time, no? Or we could attempt to exert more power over that if developers allow us to make that choice.

Rebekah: Like as a journalist, if Iâm struggling to answer a question, there are a lot of things Iâll do to get an answer. Ask people. Research primary sources online. Read newspapers. Send emails, make calls, talk to experts, look into communities. Asking Claude or ChatGPT or whatever doesnât even occur. Like, it never once enters onto my list of, âthis is a potential way to find a solution.â So I have questions about why it was even a consideration for them at all.

But also, so many people in my life use ChatGPT without even thinking about it. Like, itâs a non-issue to them, not remotely controversial. I donât know these devs personally, I donât know what they know about the harms it perpetuates. I feel like they should know based on their previously stated politics, but, people are inscrutable!

I guess at minimum we can say they know now. I will expect a disclosure on their next game confirming no AI was used. If I do not see that disclosure I will not buy it. Not because I adamantly refuse to play any game with even a drop of it in there ever, but because given their past actions I cannot trust that a game with no such disclosure did not use it in ways I do not anticipate or am not comfortable with.

John: Again, Iâm just thinking about being a developer using the tools developers have access to. They are all riddled with AI. Try avoiding that shit in Photoshop.

Ash: And Iâm saying if, because of the structures theyâre forced into, devs are required to use AI in the process of their development, I can understand and possibly forgive its use. But you gotta tell me so I can make that choice myself.

John: Itâs even harder, because Steam directly tells them not to declare its use in coding.

Rebekah: That is another thing thatâs worth mentioning though. Unityâs stuffed with AI crap. And Unity, critically, was apparently very unhelpful to them when they asked for assistance solving their coding problems. Unity I think deserves a big olâ pile of heat for its role in this as well.

Carolyn: This is why I think that if we donât set a very clear expectation of no AI use, it will just continue to seep into everything even more and more. So yes, that means putting pressure on Unity to not build it into their tools, and if they continue to do so, it means pressuring devs not to use Unity. And so on. Obviously the people with all the money at the top of these institutions want it employed so they can save money on labor. We have to tell them thatâs not gonna fly.

John: Someone said to me today that going after the developers is like going after smokers, and that we should instead be going after the companies that release the poison. I see their point, but also think you have to explain to smokers why smoking is so incredibly dangerous to them and those around them. But to take their point, it would be far more effective to shame Valve into including coding AI declarations than to pressure each individual developer into publicly shaming themselves.

Ash: I understand AIâs ubiquity makes that hard, but if we want to get rid of this shit or at least discourage its use, we gotta draw the line somewhere. But I agree that Unity, Valve, etc needs to come up more in this discussion.

Rebekah: This is not to remotely take the blame off House House, but for this to work we need to find ways to get more AAA studios on board, and I donât know how we do that. Not to say we should throw our hands in the air and give up, I just donât know where to begin pressuring major companies. Boycotts famously are not meaningfully impactful at the AAA level. I would really like to see people organize around finding solutions to that. Ash: I think it means getting a developer like House House to say âBecause of this, weâre gonna use Godot going forward.â Which I understand is incredibly easy for a non-developer to say. Ash: I think they know pretty well at this point. Rebekah: Sure, but again I think thereâs a difference between a lot of people yelling on social media and emailing them for comment, and someone who loved their game emailing them to tell them how this personally affects them

Rebekah: I honestly donât know what to do about it. It certainly calls into question whether the idea of âGOTYâ describes some sort of award or honor I am conferring on something for excellence, or if it just describes the best thing I played this year.

I cannot deny that it remains the best thing I played this year. The best experience I had. Iâd be lying to myself and everyone else to pretend it wasnât. But I also am not going to sit here and say this hasnât changed how I now look back on that experience, nor do I feel comfortable showing up to a Kotaku GOTY discussion to loudly go to bat for it as something deserving of a website-wide honor. Then again, how many other things that weâll argue for this year used AI in their development, and we donât know about it?

Where I sit right now is that I will probably pitch a piece solely on Big Walk for end-of-year discussions talking both about what it meant to me and why it was the best thing I played, and also how thatâs changed now. But as it stands I donât want to fight for it to win something thatâs seen as an âaward.â My feelings may change in either direction in the next few weeks. This is still pretty fresh. Ash: I still want to play it with yâall though, I think itâs worth at least that.

#3728. Under pressure, Big Walk studio reveals it used generative AI "sparingly" while making its hit 2026 game

"It has become a matter of public interest."

Australian developer House House has revealed it used generative AI "sparingly" to help make celebrated, indie, multiplayer puzzle game Big Walk.

In a statement sent to Aftermath - following a judging fallout related to the Independent Games Festival - House House revealed it had used large language models primarily to help debug the game's code.

"In the final stretch of Big Walk's development, LLMs were used sparingly by House House to help work through difficult technical challenges and bugs," the developer said. "In some cases, snippets from LLM responses were copied as a starting point to be modified into game code - we'd estimate that well under 0.1 percent of Big Walk's code had anything to do with this usage, and generative AI was not used in any other context when making the game."

House House added: "The primary use case for House House's use of LLMs was to research, via chatbots, issues we encountered with third-party code."

The studio's revelation comes after a sizeable number of IGF jurors - 19 of them - issued a statement saying they would not vote for any game that used generative AI during its development. This was done after seeing "a significant increase" in entry submissions involving generative AI use, which "set off some fairly intense discussion and disagreement across the judge and jury pools". And rather than not vote for these in silence, a collection of jurors decided to take a public stand.

House House hadn't disclosed Big Walk generative AI use anywhere before disclosing it for its IGF submission. "We have not made any disclosure on Steam as the platform does not request disclosure of code or chatbot usage," the studio explained. "We are posting this disclosure as it has become a matter of public interest."

House House added: "This is not an endorsement of, or argument for, the use of AI tools, however minimal. We have some concern that voluntary disclosures like this might contribute to the normalisation of this technology, or its treatment as 'inevitable'. We support the work of those who are trying to limit the harm generative AI is doing to video games and our world, and apologise that Big Walk's LLM usage may not meet their standards.

"Big Walk was developed without an internal AI usage policy in place, and we consider that lack of policy a failure. We will work to have a more comprehensive policy going forwards."

It's a revelation that's likely to leave a taint of some degree on one of this year's brightest stars - a game Eurogamer awarded a full five stars to in its Big Walk review.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Pixar movies have been entertaining audiences for decades, especially the Toy Story franchise. We were treated to another adventure with everyone's favorite toys when Toy Story 5 hit theaters earlier this year, with the project now streaming with a Disney+ subscription. I've been wondering why that army of Buzz Lightyears spent so much of the film wandering around the woods, and now we finally have some answers behind that narrative choice.

Toy Story 5 reviews were positive, and plenty of folks liked the running gag of all the Buzz Lightyears roaming around the woods together. During an interview with Gold Derby, director/writer Andrew Stanton got real about why the squad of Buzz toys spent so much time in the wilderness. As he explained:

We wanted them in the woods because then they wouldn't be constantly bumping into humans. And we just needed a nondescript shortcut to get wherever they're going. But then somebody in my story group drew a Buzz Lightyear petting a bunny, and it was like watching an actor choose something that was instinctual. We all knew that deep down under that tough exterior that Buzz has such a soft heart. And animals can sense when you're kind. And it just made sense that they would get along with cute woodland creatures.

Honestly, this makes a great deal of sense. We all know that toys in the animated franchise play dead whenever humans encounter them, hiding the secret that they're actually alive. So when Toy Story 5 brought in an entire group of new Buzz Lightyears, they had to be put in a setting that allowed the action figures to continue guarding that secret.

Toy Story 5 made fans appreciate Jessie, but the running gag of all the Buzz Lightyears was a delightful side plot during the movie's 102-minute runtime. It was heartwarming to see the toys connecting with various animals in the woods, which also served as an A+ reference to Bambi. As the filmmaker went on to share:

And there's something meta about woodland creatures and animation and Bambi, and it just felt like all these roads met at the same time to the degree that when we were putting the scene together and it was cracking us up privately by putting Bambi's ['Love Is a Song'] in there. I said we should look into getting the rights because it's the one time I would be willing to go off script composer-wise, much to Randy Newman's chagrin. But to really sell the joke and to sell the moment, it's just this kind of animation history.

The Toy Story franchise is known for including easter eggs to other Disney projects, so the fact that the fifth movie went full Bambi shouldn't have come as much of surprise. Still, I'm glad that we got some answers about why the Buzz squad was kept in the woods for the majority of the movie.

Toy Story 5 is streaming now on Disney+ as part of the 2026 movie release list. We'll just have to see if the House of Mouse moves forward with a sixth installment of the beloved property.

Yes, this fits with Sony's broader pullback from PC, but the real reason the app is "retiring" is a simple lack of interest.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Sony took another step back from the PC today, announcing that the PlayStation Plus app for PC will be "retiring" on December 10. I can't really blame it for this one, though: Almost nobody was actually using it.

"PlayStation believes in providing high-quality experiences to our players, and we regularly review offerings to ensure we are focusing on experiences our members value most," Sony wrote at the tail-end of a PlayStation Blog update detailing the PlayStation Plus game lineup for November.

"With a very small number of eligible PlayStation Plus Premium members (less than 0.4%) using the PlayStation Plus app on PC, making this change allows us to focus on enhancing high-quality experiences that more of our members want to use. As a result, the PlayStation Plus cloud streaming app on PC will no longer be available."

The end of the app seems to fit pretty well with Sony's recent about-face on PC gaming: After a brief period of enthusiasm for bringing its big exclusives to PC, Sony began a walkback earlier this year, shifting its focus back to consoles exclusives. It hasn't explicitly acknowledged or explained the change in strategy, but as PC Gamer's Morgan Park wrote in May, the thing speaks for itself: Rather like Xbox "recommitting" to its console, "Sony is responding to a waning interest in consoles by reinforcing its 'narrative singleplayer games' as system sellers once again.

"Multiplayer games like the upcoming Marvel Tōkon will still come to PC, but if you want to play the next prestige action game from the likes of Naughty Dog or Insomniac, you'll need a PS5," Morgan wrote. Or, when the time comes, a PlayStation 6.

Similar to Xbox cloud streaming, the PlayStation Plus app on PC was really more noteworthy for the selection of older PlayStation games it offered to PC gamers, rather than major new releases. Given that, I think the end has come for exactly the reason Sony cited: Not due to any strategic realignment, but simply because nobody's using it in the first place.

#3724. Where to catch Bloodgill in DREADMOOR

While attempting to fix all tuning forks in DREADMOOR, Malcolm will meet the enigmatic Father Matthias, who will task him with catching two Bloodgill fish if he wants to finish his quest.

The fish’s location, however, won’t be marked on your map, making it a matter of knowing where to search. To help you save both fuel and time, here’s where to catch Bloodgill in DREADMOOR, as well as what you must do after giving them to Father Matthias.

Contrary to what you might imagine, you won’t be able to find Bloodgill spawns close to Father Matthias’ island in DREADMOOR. Instead, you can catch the fish by heading to the spot marked below, located south of The Slough’s Trading Post. The fish will become way more common after you reach the Big Hollow, though, and will be easy to spot close to the post’s new location.

Like all other predatory catches, the Bloodgill can be angled with both the Rainbow Fin and Flaming Belly baits. You can check out the items needed to craft both below, as well as get the Flaming Belly recipe by purchasing it from Gill and Bozur for 80 Coins at the trading post. To see how to unlock all other baits, take a look at our How to get all bait recipes in DREADMOOR guide.

After giving the fish to Father Matthias, you can then progress through the quest by heading to the top of the island and placing both the tuning fork prongs and the other required items at its ritual site. Make sure to also sleep before heading back to the trading post to avoid the dangers of nighttime.

#3723. World of Warcraft: Forever might live officially on PC, but people are playing it on phones and handhelds already

If you're a World of Warcraft: Forever player you're almost certainly having your free time drained as you chain yourself to your desktop PC to play the game, or maybe a laptop. But for a small selection of true enthusiasts, the game is already working on mobile and handheld devices.

One such person showing off WoW: Forever on the go is none other than director of publishing at Larian, Michael Douse, who took to Twitter to show off the MMO being played on an AYN Thor device. For those who don't know, this is a fancy android handheld console, a sort of beefed up DS for the modern handheld aficionado.

"Arguably too many layers of abstraction," writes Douse. In the picture he posted, you can see the player character viewable on the Thor's top screen, while the map, text chat, skill UI, and buffs viewable on the bottom. It looks pretty cool, and is made possible due to JReese702's Github mod you can download at your leisure.

Arguably too many layers of abstraction pic.twitter.com/VjW0IX00Gg

But it's not the only mo-bell at the ball. Another Github WoW: Forever mod, WolkaraForever, gets the game playable on the iPhone Duo. As highlighted by CEO of esports company 100 Thieves Alex Wechsler on Twitter, the game looks to be ported pretty well to the phone, with mobile touchscreen controls viewable on both sides of the screen. Be warned though, as confirmed by Wechsler in a Twitter reply, it'll get your phone running hot.

As a father of 2 kids and always having wanted to play WOW, I’ve finally found a way 🥹 pic.twitter.com/eIVn0gn1WC

This coming alongside World of Warcraft: Forever's built-in (and very good) controller support could mean the game has real potential to spread far and wide across the vast array of different hardware out there. Blizzard has already hinted at plans of porting the game to other platforms, so who knows? Maybe we can expect an official mobile port to tread the path paved by these community-made mods.

#3722. How To Get A Sleeping Bag In World Of Warcraft: Forever

World of WarcraftWorld of Warcraft: Forever

If you’ve been partying up with others in World of Warcraft: Forever, you’ve probably seen a weird sleeping bag item being used by your teammates. You may have even been encouraged to use it yourself, and gotten a little EXP boost for your trouble. Now, having snuggled up in the sleeping bag with four of your dungeoning buddies, maybe you want this nap device for yourself and your own leveling journey. I am here to tell you how to get it. The journey is not without pain and sacrifice.

The Cozy Sleeping Bag is an item first introduced in WoW‘s Season of Discovery. It has unlimited uses on a one-hour-long cooldown. When you use it (the cast takes 15 whole seconds), you place a sleeping bag on the ground. If you stand still on top of it, your character will lay down after a few seconds and take a nap. In this state, you’ll gain a stack of a buff once every minute up to three stacks, with each stack giving you a 1-percent bonus to EXP earned that lasts through death, for two hours. So in total, you spend a little over three minutes to receive a 3-percent bump to EXP gained for two hours. The best part is that you can share this with your party members, so one sleeping bag will give your whole group a buff if everyone takes a nap together.

That said, given how long it takes to obtain, it’s…kind of a worthless reward. You’ll spend about the same amount of time you save in leveling just running all over the place to obtain the bag in the first place. It’s not a toy, so it takes up a precious inventory slot, too. That said, you do also get a 12-slot bag from the questline, which feels truly luxurious early in the game. And you can use this as an opportunity to pick up a bunch of useful flight points you’ll be happy to have later. As Horde, I grabbed flight points at places like Grom’gol, Booty Bay, Tarren Mill, Sunrock Retreat, and Hammerfall. I also did the early steps of this quest simultaneously with getting the Night Watchman’s Torch, which helped “save time” (if you can call any bit of this time-saving).

You’ll need to be at least level 14 to start this quest. Be warned, you will end up running into high-level areas to finish this, and will probably die a lot in the process. My general tip for this is to stay on the main roads whenever you can, as monsters tend to avoid them. However, some areas (like Stranglethorn Vale) will have monsters that will aggro you from off the path, and other places you’ll run through are PvP zones, so you may have to improvise. Just don’t be deceived into thinking that cross-country hikes are the best idea.

The first two steps are the only ones that are different depending on whether you’re Alliance or Horde. Both factions will have to complete both steps, just in reverse order from one another.

Alliance will start in Westfall. For Horde, this is your step two, so be prepared to come back to this momentarily. In Westfall, head for coordinates 37, 50 (you can see coordinates in the top right corner under your minimap, no add-ons required). Alliance can easily reach here from Stormwind as part of their normal questing journey, but Horde have a rougher time. Take the zeppelin from Orgrimmar to Stranglethorn Vale, then go north from Grom’gol through Darkshore and turn west when you can to Westfall. Beware, because Stranglethorn is full of high-level monsters that will aggro you if you breathe within a mile of them, and Darkshore and Westfall are full of Alliance NPCs. You can also swim the shore from Grom’gol up to the Westfall beach, if you prefer.

You’re looking to get to the middle of the Alexston Farmstead just southeast of the Gold Coast Quarry. There are a bunch of harvester enemies running around that may make things difficult, but if you can get clear of them you can interact with a Nailed Plank in a burnt-out cart. Alliance will pick up “…and that note you found” and Horde will get “Stepping Stones.”

Horde, you’ll start with this next step. Alliance, this is your step two. This one is in the Barrens. You’re looking for a burnt watchtower, at coordinates 46, 74 or so. Horde can get here easily by flying to Camp Taurajo (or walking from Orgrimmar, Crossroads, or Thunder Bluff) and taking the main road through the Barrens south. For Alliance, it’s a rougher journey, but you can make it by heading south from Darkshore (which is reachable by boat from Stormwind), through Ashenvale, and then down south further into the Barrens. At the watchtower, Horde will pick up the quest “…and that note you found” and Alliance will get “Stepping Stones.” Horde will then need to follow the previous step to Westfall to get their next quest.

Once you have “Stepping Stones,” the path is the same for both factions.

“Stepping Stones” takes you to Stonetalon Mountains, which Horde can get to from The Barrens and Alliance can get to…well, also from The Barrens, which is probably where you are if you just did the previous quest. Alliance have a hub at Stonetalon Peak, and Horde have Sunrock Retreat, but both groups will need to go past Sunrock Retreat and find a little path up into the mountains that lies just to the north of the outpost.

Follow the path carefully upward until you reach a small campsite with a fire, and a Pocket Litter you can interact with on top of a box. Finishing this quest will get you a 12-slot bag (yes!) and will let you pick up the next step, “Scramble.”

“Scramble”‘s turn-in point isn’t far away at all, but before you go, try to interact with the campfire. There’s a weird little quest you can do here called “Rekindle” that will restart the fire with the tinderbox and wood you got from the last quest. However, this quest was bugged for me when I did it and I was unable to click on the campfire, and this seems like a common problem a lot of people are experiencing. It will likely be patched in the future, but if it’s bugged when you reach it, don’t sweat it. You’re genuinely not missing any rewards and it’s not necessary to get the sleeping bag.

Campfire or no, head due north and up the hill, walking carefully so as not to fall down the cliff (if you do, no biggie, there’s a path that will let you climb back up easily). From the top you should be able to see the next objective, a Mound of Dirt, so jump over that way and turn in the quest, picking up “Wet job.”

Time to continent-hop again. You’re going back to Eastern Kingdoms, this time to Loch Modan. For Alliance, this is a short-ish run, and not a dangerous one. You can either start in Ironforge and walk south through Dun Morogh into Loch Modan, or go from Stormwind via boat at Menethil Harbor to Wetlands, and then had southeast through the mountain tunnel into Loch Modan.

Horde, this is another rough one. You’ll need to start in Undercity and run through Tirisfall Glades, exiting to the southwest into Silverpine Forest. Follow the path further south into Hillsbrad Foothills, continuing east into Arathi Highlands, across the southern bridge into Wetlands, and then finally through the mountain tunnel into Loch Modan. You will absolutely run into Alliance guards along the way and have to deal with PvP, there’s no way around it. Just corpse-run when you can and do your best.

Either way, you’ll want to end up at the Stonewrought Dam, which is at the very north end of the eponymous Loch of Loch Modan. You’ve got to climb atop the dam itself and walk across until you see a campsite of sorts on a ledge overlooking Wetlands. Once you’re in the right spot, descend onto the ledge above the stone heads and interact with the Eagle Figurine to complete your quest and pick up the next one, “Eagle’s Fist.”

Just one more step to go, and fortunately, it’s not too far away. Horde and Alliance alike will want to head north, back through Wetlands and Arathi Highlands toward Hillsbrad Foothills. On the border between Arathi and Hillsbrad is the Thoradin Wall, and this is your destination. Follow the wall north until you see a broken cart. The cart is on the Hillsbrad side of the wall, but this is a little easier to do at lower levels if you walk up the Arathi side and then go through the gap in the wall near the cart to cross over, as there are no monsters on the Arathi side.

You can use that cart to climb up the wall. There’s a bit of a platforming puzzle here. First climb on the weird cylinder thing, jump to the board that’s jutting out on the side, then up the cart to the wall. Then just follow the path you can take up the crumbling wall stones (start your climb on the low far left stone) until you see the camp ahead of you. Interact with the hanging Messenger Bag to finish “Eagle’s Fist” and pick up “This Must Be the Place.” Then, click on the Hastily Rolled-up Satchel to finish the last quest and get your sleeping bag at last. Congrats!

Since Sir Patrick Stewart’s passing, I have spent a great deal of time reading stories from his co-stars about his work and impact. It’s lovely to see tributes continue to pour in, but the sentiments that have truly hit me in my feels have come from Ian McKellen, Stewart's longtime best friend (and sometimes on-screen nemesis). While Sir McKellen broke his silence weeks ago, he just shared additional thoughts on his late comrade, and I may or may not need a tissue.

While Stewart and McKellen battled on the big screen as X-Men's Professor X and Magneto, respectively, the two seem inseparable in real life. They were actually so close that McKellen even officiated Stewart’s wedding to Sunny Ozell in 2013. So, when the actor stopped by Entertainment Tonight to promote his movie, Ebenezer, he got a chance to reflect on his friendship with Stewart, and his comments are just too sweet:

Well, what I thought about Sir Patrick of late is because he did his own version of Christmas Carol. He was a one-man show. He played all the characters. He did it on Broadway and did it on London’s West End a number of times. I think he toured with it. It’s a big part of his life. I just remember his friendship and his - A good man. Serious-minded. And always looking to make the world a better place, and he achieved that.

I think everyone would be better off having a friend who speaks about them as lovingly as McKellen discusses Stewart. To put it simply, the two were the definition of friendship goals, and the seasoned actors elevated everyone around them. I can't imagine it's easy for McKellen not having his good friend around, but I love that he's choosing to remember him in such a positive way.

Of course, given McKellen’s role in Ebezener as Jacob Marley, it makes sense that his friend would be on his mind. Stewart's take on A Christmas Carol still serves as a high point in his career and a benchmark for stage acting in general. It seems I'm not the only one who is feeling a a way about this tribute either based on the comments of the Instagram video. I think toriyikes sums it best: “Making me cry in the afternoon!” Fans may agree after watch ingthe video below:

A post shared by Entertainment Tonight (@entertainmenttonight)

Shortly after Patrick Stewart's death was reported, Ian McKellen took to X to share a sentimental message. In it, the star reflected on his and Stewart's time serving at the Royal Shakespeare Company and discussed their subsequent work and endearing friendship.

While Stewart was greatly known for his work as an actor, McKellen’s words were a a sweet reminder that he was so much more. Yes, he was “serious-minded,” but he was also always up for a laugh and even gave his own eulogy back in 2015 at a Just for Laughs gala. There's a reason his roles as Professor X and Jean-Luc Picard are still iconic, and it's because the compassion that he put into the world. Just as McKellen said, he made it a little better, and that's something we should all remember.

Of course, it should be noted that we will the two X-Men alums together one more time when Avengers: Doomsday hits the 2026 schedule on December 18. The movie will now mark Stewart's final on-screen performance following his death at 86 due to Alzheimer's disease and Lewy body dementia. Trailers have already teased that Stewart's Professor X and McKellen's Magneto will share the screen again, and I'm not sure I'm prepared for that reunion.

I'm confident that Patrick Stewart's final turn as the X-Men's leader will be satisfying and that his body of work as a whole will stand the test of time. More than that, though, if the comments from Ian McKellen and so many others are anything to go by, Stewart's kind spirit won't be forgotten either.
